paras: The lynching of Reddy McDonald was the hanging of a jailed man by vigilantes at Sidney, Nebraska, in the early hours of Sunday, April 3, 1881. About thirty men took him from his cell and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard; a coroner's jury found him killed by persons unknown. A Cheyenne Daily Leader dispatch calling him "a noted cut-throat" ran in papers across the country.

An Omaha dispatch traced Sidney's new vigilance committee, formed to drive out "thieves, cut-throats, and desperadoes," to an attack on the lawyer W. H. Michael. Tom Ryan, a former deputy under Sheriff Howard, had stabbed Michael the preceding Wednesday and escaped. The committee then jailed some men it called desperate characters and warned others to leave; the Leader's wire put the number jailed on Friday, April 1, at sixteen.

McDonald, called "Watson" in one Chicago dispatch, was described as head musician at Joe Lane's dance house or, by the Omaha Daily Bee, as a bar-tender. The Leader said he had tried to kill Deputy Sheriff McIntosh during his arrest; the Omaha dispatch added that he had tried to shoot the jailer and had helped Ryan escape. The Bee said he had also threatened to kill Judge Neubauer once released.

According to the Bee, the Vigilantes met and decided to put him out of the way before his release. On Saturday night about thirty men told the jailer they were bringing back the escaped Ryan, rushed in when the door opened, and brought McDonald out in his night clothes. The Leader adds that he was asleep and was dragged out in his underclothes and stocking feet.

The men led him to the court-house yard, threw a rope over the limb of a tree, and tied his hands and feet. The Leader reported that he "begged piteously for his life" and was strangled rather than having his neck broken, dying after fully fifteen minutes. The men then left in small groups, and the body was found hanging in front of the court house on Sunday.

The coroner cut the body down shortly after daylight, and the inquest returned a verdict of "killed by persons to the jury unknown." McDonald's funeral on April 4 drew what the Leader called "a large number of sympathizers," a fact it said had caused much comment. The Bee reported that prominent citizens held an indignation meeting that Sunday afternoon.

The Leader's April 4 dispatch said the other fifteen prisoners would be horsewhipped and banished one each evening. The wire said Ryan would be lynched when caught, and that two more prisoners accused of murder might be. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial of the men who hanged McDonald appears in the coverage.

The first report, a Leader special from Sidney on April 3, ran the next morning in the New-York Tribune, the Chicago Tribune and other dailies. Headlines treated it as frontier justice: "Lynch Law in Nebraska" in the New-York Tribune and Daily Kennebec Journal, "Making Good Men by Lynch Law" in the St. Paul Daily Globe. The wire reached Sacramento, Salt Lake City and Deer Lodge, Montana, and most reprints kept its line that more prisoners would be "made into good men by lynching them." Weeklies ran briefs into mid-April, the Somerset Press under "For the Good of the Community."

The Leader's own April 5 story, "Sidney's Six," dwelt on the slow strangling as "horrible in the extreme." The Omaha dispatch in the Chicago Tribune called the committee "composed of the best men in Sidney." The Bee called it a "summary act of vengeance" yet set out the vigilantes' grounds. None of the reports gives McDonald's race.

The vigilantes' stated grounds differ by source. The wire said he was planning to break jail, and the Iron County Register that he tried to free the prisoners. The longer regional accounts instead cited his alleged attacks on officers, help to Ryan and threats. Wire reports say "an early hour this morning" on April 3, the Omaha accounts "Saturday night," the same night.

bases: A band of vigilantes took a prisoner from the county jail and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard (A2, A13, A18).

About thirty vigilantes took McDonald from jail by a ruse and hanged him (A18), the coroner's jury found him killed by persons unknown (A13), and the men claimed he was a dangerous prisoner planning escape or revenge (A2, A14, A18).

The Leader's Sidney wire (A2, A4), the Leader's own longer account (A13), an Omaha dispatch (A14) and the Omaha Bee (A18) agree that he was taken from jail and hanged in the court-house yard, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Leader's Sidney wire
accounts.gist: Vigilantes took the 'noted cut-throat' from the county jail early April 3 and hanged him because he was discovered planning to break jail; he was one of sixteen desperadoes jailed Friday.

accounts.label: Cheyenne Daily Leader, follow-up
accounts.gist: He had tried to kill Deputy Sheriff McIntosh at his arrest; the mob dragged him out in his underclothes and strangled him slowly; the inquest found persons unknown; many sympathizers attended his funeral.

accounts.label: Omaha dispatch (Chicago Tribune)
accounts.gist: A vigilance committee formed after Ryan's attack on Michael hanged 'Watson McDonald' Saturday night; he had shot at a deputy, tried to shoot the jailer and helped Ryan escape.

accounts.label: Omaha Daily Bee
accounts.gist: About thirty Vigilantes, having met and decided to act before he could be released, tricked the jailer by claiming to return Ryan and hanged him; prominent citizens held an indignation meeting.

framing.detail: The Leader wire, carried widely on April 4-5, called him 'a noted cut-throat' and said more prisoners would be 'made into good men by lynching them'.
Headlines 'Making Good Men by Lynch Law' and 'For the Good of the Community'; the Omaha dispatch called the committee 'the best men in Sidney'.
The Cheyenne Leader called the strangling 'horrible in the extreme' and noted the sympathizers at the funeral, while also reporting the plan to drive out the rest of the 'gang'.
The Omaha Bee called it 'a ghastly affair' and a 'summary act of vengeance' but set out the vigilantes' grounds and said the result 'might have been expected'.
